items.paragraph: Counterfactual history, the study of what might have happened had some event gone differently, is often dismissed as a parlour game for historians with too much time. The dismissal overlooks that every causal claim in history is already a counterfactual. To say that a drought caused a rebellion is to say that without the drought the rebellion would not have occurred, or would have come later or smaller; a historian who refuses to think about alternatives cannot weigh causes at all. Asking what was genuinely possible for the people involved, given what they knew and could do, is not fantasy but part of explaining why events took the course they did.

items.paragraph: Artificial light at night is usually discussed as a loss for astronomers and stargazers, but its larger effects fall on other species. Many animals use darkness and the cycle of light as information: moths navigate by it, some birds time their migration by it, and newly hatched turtles find the sea by moving towards the brighter horizon over the water. A lit coastline or city confuses these cues, so that insects circle lamps until they are exhausted, birds strike illuminated buildings and hatchlings crawl inland. What makes the problem unusual among forms of pollution is that it can be reversed almost instantly: unlike a poisoned river, a lit landscape is restored the moment the lights are dimmed or shielded. The difficulty is not technical but a matter of persuading people that darkness has value.

items.paragraph: Defenders of reality television often say that nothing in it is scripted, and in a narrow sense they may be right: the participants choose their own words. But a programme is made in the edit as much as on location. Hundreds of hours of footage are cut to a few, and the choice of which glance to keep, which remark to place after which, and what music to lay underneath can turn an ordinary disagreement into a feud or a tired participant into a villain. The question to ask of such shows is therefore not whether they are scripted but how they are assembled, and that is a question their defenders rarely answer.

items.paragraph: Recorded laughter on television comedies is often mocked as a crude instruction to the audience, a machine telling viewers when something is funny. items.paragraph: Business writing often treats being first to market as a decisive advantage, and the stories it tells are memorable: the pioneer that defined a category and never let go. Yet such stories are drawn disproportionately from survivors. Pioneers that created a market and were then overtaken by better-funded or more careful followers are forgotten, or are remembered as footnotes to the followers' success, so the sample from which the lesson is drawn is tilted in its favour. Followers also enjoy real benefits: they can learn from the pioneer's mistakes, wait for customers to understand the product and adopt technology that has become cheaper. This does not mean that entering first is never valuable; where customers face high costs of switching, an early lead can harden into dominance. It means that the advantage is conditional, and that the anecdotes usually offered for it cannot establish how often it holds.

items.paragraph: Newspaper obituaries have long followed a convention of discretion: the dead are praised for their achievements, while their failings are passed over or hinted at in phrases that knowing readers decode. The convention is defended as kindness to grieving families, and kindness is a real consideration. But an obituary is also the first draft of a public record, often consulted later by people who never knew the subject. When it omits the serious harm a powerful person did, it does not merely spare feelings; it misinforms everyone who relies on it afterwards. items.paragraph: For decades the lesson drawn from wrongful convictions was that a witness's confidence tells us little about whether the witness is right: jurors are swayed by a certain voice, and certainty is no guarantee of accuracy. That lesson is now being refined rather than overturned. When an identification is made for the first time, from a fairly conducted line-up, and the witness's confidence is recorded on the spot, high confidence turns out to be a reasonably good sign of accuracy, and hesitant identifications deserve real doubt. The trouble lies in what happens afterwards. Confidence grows with feedback, rehearsal and the passage of months, so that the certainty displayed in a courtroom may bear little relation to the uncertainty felt at the original moment. Confidence, then, is informative evidence, but only if it is captured before the process of investigation has had a chance to manufacture it.

items.paragraph: Firms that replace telephone agents with chatbots often report that customer satisfaction scores barely move, and conclude that customers do not mind. Those who give up rarely answer a survey about an exchange they abandoned, and some of them quietly take their business elsewhere. Steady scores may therefore show only that bots cope with easy cases, while the frustrations of hard cases fall outside what is being counted.

items.paragraph: Modern dictionaries describe themselves as records of how a language is used rather than rulebooks for how it ought to be used. (1) If enough speakers use a word in a new sense, the new sense goes in, whatever earlier editors or schoolteachers might have thought of it. (2) Many readers, however, open a dictionary precisely to be told what is correct, and a record that merely reports usage can seem to have abandoned them. (3) The usage note is the dictionary's answer to this tension. Rather than ruling on a disputed word, it reports that some careful writers avoid it, or that it may strike certain readers as informal, and leaves the decision with the user. (4) Such notes are descriptive in form, since attitudes towards a word are themselves a fact about the language, but in practice they steer readers as firmly as any rule. A writer warned that a usage annoys some readers will usually avoid it, and the warning, repeated across editions, can help keep the disapproval alive.

items.paragraph: It seems obvious that famines happen when there is not enough food. Yet several major famines have occurred in regions where the total supply of food was not much lower than in normal years, and some while food was being exported. What collapsed was not the harvest but the ability of particular groups to obtain food: labourers whose wages fell, artisans whose customers vanished, herders whose animals lost value as grain prices rose. A famine, on this view, is less a shortage of food than a failure of access to it, concentrated on those whose means of buying or growing it have broken down. This does not mean harvests are irrelevant, for a poor harvest is often what sets the collapse in motion; it means that counting the grain is not enough to predict who will starve.

items.paragraph: When people work together on a shared task, the total effort of the group is often less than the sum of what each member would produce alone. (1) Part of the shortfall is simply a matter of coordination, since people pulling on the same rope rarely pull at exactly the same moment. (2) But a larger part seems to come from a quieter change in motivation. When individual contributions cannot be seen, each member can ease off a little without being noticed, and many do. (3) Appeals to try harder therefore tend to fail, because each member assumes that the appeal is addressed to someone else. What works better is to make contributions visible, or to give each person a part of the task that is recognisably their own. (4) Groups, in short, do not make people lazy so much as they make laziness invisible, and the remedy is to restore visibility.
